Abstract:

Machine learning methods have become increasingly popular for modeling complex systems across science, engineering, and finance. However, purely data-driven approaches often suffer from limitations such as data inefficiency, lack of physical consistency, and poor extrapolation when applied to problems governed by differential equations. Classical numerical methods, although rigorous, can be computationally expensive and dependent on structured discretization schemes. This thesis addresses these challenges by developing kernel-based machine learning frameworks, with a particular focus on Least Square Support Vector Machines (LS-SVM) and their physics-informed extension, as reliable and efficient meshless numerical methods. The study begins with a comprehensive analysis of kernel-based learning and LS-SVM formulations. Building on this foundation, a Physics-Informed Least Square Support Vector Machine (PI-LSSVM) framework is developed by embedding governing equations, boundary conditions, and physical constraints directly into the learning and optimization structure. The proposed framework combines kernel-based approximation with physical consistency while avoiding deep neural architectures and nonconvex optimization. The effectiveness of the proposed methods is demonstrated through applications to higher-order differential equations, option pricing models including the Black&ndashScholes, Constant Elasticity of Variance models, and nonlinear wave dynamics. Numerical experiments and comparative studies show that PI-LSSVM achieves improved accuracy, stability, and data efficiency compared to conventional kernel-based and classical numerical methods. The results establish physics-informed kernel learning as a robust and versatile approach for solving real life problems.
